items.title: Riyadh airport hit again after deadly Houthi missile attack, Saudi authorities say
items.originalTitle: Riyadh airport hit again after deadly Houthi missile attack, Saudi authorities say
items.summary: A projectile hit a passenger terminal at the airport in Riyadh on Sunday, the day after a deadly missile attack on the facility carried out by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebel group killed 13 people. An unidentified projectile hit terminal 4 at King Khalid international airport, starting a fire, killing one person and injuring 11, according to Saudi civil aviation authorities. Air defences also intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of the airport. It was the latest of several attacks on the airport in the past week. The escalating attacks threatened to draw more countries into the Yemen conflict and further widen the regional fallout of the US-Iran war, which has already spread to Lebanon and Iraq. In a post on X, the British embassy in Saudi Arabia advised against all but essential travel to the cities of Jeddah and Dammam and to avoid almost all airports. After Saturday’s strike on Riyadh airport, the US president, Donald Trump, said he was weighing whether to join the Saudi military campaign in Yemen, telling reporters: “We’re going to look into it.” The Iran-allied Houthis claimed to have launched several attacks on the airport, including the attack on Saturday, which killed 13 people and injured more than 300 – the deadliest attack on a Gulf country since the war with Iran started in March and an apparent escalation in the Houthis’ war with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government that Riyadh sponsors. In response to the attack, Saudi authorities extended the closure of the airport and said schools would be moved online until Thursday.

evidenceRecords.text: The U.S. Navy published a Sources Sought Notice concerning SSN(X) late in the morning on October 9th, seeking information from industry on manufacturing capabilities for the submarine meant to succeed the vaunted Virginia -class fast attack boats.

The notice represents one of the initial steps of getting a program off of the drawing board and into the manufacturing cycle, preceding the likely service entry date of the new class of submarines by over a decade.

The primary purpose of such a notice aims to give the U.S. Navy feedback from industry partners, in this case about which “interested and capable” U.S. shipyards can meet the needs for production and support of SSN(X).

As stipulated in the notice, interested prime shipyards must be capable of completing the advanced manufacturing steps present in the process of producing a submarine, which includes the capabilities for “executing complex manufacturing, complete hull fabrication, modular outfitting, precision systems integration, reactor compartment installation, and post-delivery testing.” The Navy also seeks information on yard availability, workforce skill and availability, and the presence of key elements such as advanced machine tooling, floating dry docks, and a crane system capable of lifting entire

As such, these criteria narrow down the possible manufacturers considerably, leaving practically only two candidates in the shape of General Dynamics Electric Boat with their main yard in Groton, Connecticut, and Huntington Ingalls’ Newport News Shipbuilding with their facilities at Newport News, Virginia.

Both of these yards have extensive experience building advanced Nuclear submarines, and both currently produce Virginia-class SSNs, although General Dynamics Electric Boat remains the primary contractor.

evidenceRecords.text: The UK Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) is looking to hire an uncrewed aerial systems (UAS) expert, who would join the Airspace Regulation team as the UK looks to implement a new Airspace Modernisation Strategy.

The UAS expert is needed to help integrate the demands of diverse airspace users such as UAS, eVTOL/hybrid aircraft, as well as general, military and commercial aviation, spaceports and space launch operators.

They will perform regulatory oversight of the current airspace system to support the development of polices to integrate UAS and other new users, and assist in developing and implementing strategies and policies for airspace design, use or change.

The UAS expert will also review and scrutinise airspace proposals from a wide range of sponsors such as operators, airports, the military and spaceports, producing objective and independent assessments of the direct and consequential airspace impacts for each proposed airspace change design.
They would then lay out the conclusions of these assessments and form a key part of the CAA’s transparent decision-making process for approvals.
A sound understanding of UK airspace, air traffic operations and emerging technology developments in the aviation industry is essential for the role.

items.summary: Donald Trump has claimed that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an "energy ceasefire", with Kyiv saying it would support such a move but Moscow yet to comment. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky initially expressed surprise at the announcement, before saying Kyiv would support it if Moscow did. evidenceRecords.text: Donald Trump has claimed that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an "energy ceasefire", with Kyiv saying it would support such a move but Moscow yet to comment.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky initially expressed surprise at the announcement, before saying Kyiv would support it if Moscow did.
He also accused Russia of striking Ukrainian energy facilities after Trump's post.

Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure - which Kyiv says are vital to curtailing revenue for Moscow's war machine - so Russia can fulfil a recently-struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market.
The diesel deal, temporarily undoing sanctions on Russian imports, is attracting growing criticism.
Zelensky called it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
European officials and some US politicians, including from Trump's Republican party, have said they do not support it.

The deal is Trump's latest effort to lower domestic fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections, having spent months grappling with the political consequences of the war with Iran which has pushed up global fuel prices, particularly those for diesel.

Zelensky said it was "news" to him that an energy truce was in effect in comments to news site Axios, before writing on social media that his officials "look forward to clear details of America's dialogue with Russia".
"Ukraine is ready not to strike at Russian energy and we count on Russia's similar readiness and on the agreement of the president of the United States of America on this," he said.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now", while France, Canada and the EU also expressed support.
Zelensky later said Russia had hit a power plant in Kyiv with a drone, causing power cuts, followed by strikes on energy facilities in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.
Zelensky pledged to hold elections - despite them being suspended by the Ukrainian constitution during wartime - if Russia agreed to a 60-day total ceasefire.

The Ukrainian president previously resisted calls from the US for fresh elections, pointing to complications with holding a vote in parts of the country that are active war zones or under Russian occupation.

evidenceRecords.text: On Equity, we debate the impact of data center moratoriums and whether the AI industry has a communication problem.
It’s also noteworthy that Microsoft, earlier this year, made a similar announcement about not using NDAs.
I don’t think that getting rid of the NDAs automatically is going to make the people who opposed these data centers be like, “Great, let’s let’s do it.

I’m in.” But I think the beginning of that conversation is, “Well, we don’t even know what the heck you’re doing, because you’ve negotiated all this stuff in secret.” So it does seem like a good first step.
Sean: The larger problem here is just a communication problem, right?

This is a problem I think that goes across the entire tech industry, but it’s especially acute now, because we’re living in the era of “going direct” and “you don’t need to talk to the media, the media is dead,” etc.
And I’m not trying to beat that horse, because we’re in the media and [we] think we’re still relevant.

But we’ve seen, through a lot of the controversy and backlash to AI and data centers, that the industry just does a really poor job explaining itself, and that they are obviously and constantly frustrated with the fact that most people can’t envision a world in which this stuff is useful for them.
And that’s because, a lot of time, the [technological] ability’s not there, and in part because they’re just not explaining it well.

It’s just wild to me that we’re a year into that, and the company still doesn’t have a very good definition of it, especially considering that they released this whole multi-page PDF laying it out when they announced this, and even Tesla’s biggest fans criticized Elon Musk and Tesla for how unspecific it was.

Anthony: One of the things this has made me think about is just the narrative and this sense that for a while, it really felt like it was being pushed down our throats — this idea of, “This is inevitable, this AI-driven future, and get on board or you’re just going to be left behind.”

items.originalTitle: These execs think voice AI hasn’t reached its ChatGPT moment yet
items.summary: Every week there is a new model or a tool release that claims to sound human and converse like one. However, in reality, that might not be the case. Enterprise voice AI platform PolyAI’s CTO Shawn Wen thinks that despite the release of full-duplex models — which can speak while listening to you — voice AI doesn’t have its “ChatGPT moment” yet. “We have reached the milestone of developing full-duplex models. The next challenge is to make reasoning very fast, so that the models can fetch answers quickly and the conversation feels natural,” he told me on stage at the HumanX conference last month.

evidenceRecords.text: Every week there is a new model or a tool release that claims to sound human and converse like one.
However, in reality, that might not be the case.
Enterprise voice AI platform PolyAI’s CTO Shawn Wen thinks that despite the release of full-duplex models — which can speak while listening to you — voice AI doesn’t have its “ChatGPT moment” yet.
“We have reached the milestone of developing full-duplex models.
The next challenge is to make reasoning very fast, so that the models can fetch answers quickly and the conversation feels natural,” he told me on stage at the HumanX conference last month.

“I think the next stage will be slightly different because once the voice is good enough, like, and the customer is willing to engage with them for the first two or three turns, they start to build confidence, and over time, they will feel like I probably don’t have to talk to a human if the agent can solve my problem,” he said.
Alex Gay, CMO for meeting notetaker Otter, opined that speaker identification, intent capture, and typing that up with organizational knowledge is a key step for enabling automation.
The company is also working on digital twins that might represent people in meetings.
For that technology, he said it’s paramount that the output voice gives the same emotive expressions of talking to a human in a meeting.

“If you think about the meetings that you’re in right now, the best conversations that you have are where you can have debate, and strategic discussions, and when you feel like there’s a relationship that underpins it.
If you aren’t able to have that with an avatar, then it’s just a q and a chatbot,” Gay noted.
While voice AI models have improved, AI assistants often don’t understand users, or your meeting notetaker shows the wrong transcript or a summary.

evidenceRecords.text: Through photographs, spoken observations, drawings, and annotations, the Artemis II crew created a unique scientific record—one that is now available to the science community and the public for further study.
In addition, the Artemis II flight provided an opportunity for observation, science, and data gathering that has not existed since the Apollo Era.
During the flight, the astronauts studied the "dark side's" geology, witnessed nighttime impacts on the surface, and watched the Earth and Sun rise from the far side of the Moon.
And now, with the mission data processed, NASA has released "Artemis II: Sights & Sounds of Science, a field guide to the Artemis II Preliminary Lunar Science Report.
Explore highlights here, and find the full suite of reports and select data resources at the bottom of the page.
Who can forget the lovely picture the Artemis II astronauts took of planet Earth on Day 2 of the mission?

But for mission scientists, it was more than a pretty picture; it captured active weather systems, auroras at both poles, distinct atmospheric layers, a Saharan dust plume, zodiacal light, and city lights on the surface.
While Earth-observation satellites are crucial to science, they observe the Earth in strips rather than getting a holistic view.
Captured by the Artemis II crew during their lunar flyby on April 6, 2026, this image shows the Moon fully eclipsing the Sun.
Credit: NASA
Per the mission plan, lunar scientists asked the Artemis II crew to use the nearly hour-long total solar eclipse as they passed the Moon’s far side.
The observed flashes coincided with a planned communications loss as Integrity passed into the Moon's shadow.
The crew then sent the video they acquired to the Lunar Science Team at NASA's Johnson Space Center Mission Control Center in Houston (shown in the video above).
That data is essential to the Artemis program and its long-term objective of creating lunar habitats that will enable long-term operations on the lunar surface.
